title: Databricks Platform Tour
subtitle: Account, workspace, planes, compute, runtime, Photon, notebooks, widgets, catalogs — and first debugging
mantra: Workspace is where you work, compute is what works, DBR is the software on it, Photon makes it fast, Unity Catalog names and guards the data — debug by finding the layer first.
objectives: You can explain Databricks as a platform (not 'managed Spark') and separate account vs workspace and control vs compute plane.
You can choose between serverless, classic all-purpose, jobs compute and SQL warehouses for a given workload.
You can explain Databricks Runtime, LTS, Runtime ML and Photon — and why Photon needs no code changes.
You can write notebook code mixing Python and SQL: spark.table, spark.sql, display, magic commands and _sqldf.
You can parameterize notebooks with dbutils.widgets and modern :param / IDENTIFIER() SQL syntax.
You can explore and create catalogs, schemas and Delta tables with SHOW/DESCRIBE/CREATE/INSERT and fully qualified names.
You can debug by layer: not attached, TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND, INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES, ModuleNotFoundError, slow queries.

sections.title: What Databricks Actually Is
sections.hook: If you think "Databricks = managed Spark", every product name will feel random.

blocks.label: Think first: Workspace, Serverless, Compute, SQL Warehouse, Databricks Runtime, Photon, Notebook, Unity Catalog — 8 unrelated products?
blocks.text: No. They are **layers of one model**: where you work (workspace, notebook), what executes (compute: serverless/classic/SQL warehouse), the software on the machines (Runtime), the fast engine (Photon), and who may touch what (Unity Catalog). This chapter builds that model.
The most dangerous oversimplification is **Databricks = managed Spark**. Historically that was close to the truth. Today it is not.
Databricks is a **unified data/AI platform**: data engineering, analytics, AI/ML, governance and deployment in one environment. **Apache Spark** is still the central *execution technology* inside it.

┌──────────────────── DATABRICKS ────────────────────┐
│   Notebooks        SQL Editor        Jobs          │
│       └────────────────┼────────────────┘          │
│                        ▼                           │
│              COMPUTE  (Spark / Photon)             │
│                        ▼                           │
│              Delta / other data                    │
│                        ▼                           │
│              Cloud storage                         │
│                                                    │
│   Unity Catalog governs all of these assets        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
blocks.caption: Interfaces on top, compute in the middle, data at the bottom, governance across everything.

blocks.title: Engine vs car
blocks.text: Spark is the **engine**. Databricks is the whole car: engine, dashboard, keys and locks (governance), navigation (orchestration) and the garage that maintains it.

blocks.title: Classic trap
blocks.text: Spark is **not** a cloud provider and **not** a file format. Databricks and Spark are **not** synonyms: Spark is one of the core execution technologies *inside* Databricks.

sections.title: Account vs Workspace
sections.hook: The first boundary every exam and every admin conversation starts with.

blocks.text: Imagine a company, **ACME Corporation**, buys Databricks. At the very top sits the **Databricks account** — the organization-level boundary.
At **account level** you manage users, groups and service principals, workspaces, Unity Catalog metastores, billing and account-level policies. One account can contain **many workspaces**.

DATABRICKS ACCOUNT  (organization level)
│
├── identities (users, groups, service principals)
├── billing
├── account policies
├── Unity Catalog configuration (metastores)
│
├── Workspace A
├── Workspace B
└── Workspace C
blocks.caption: One account → many workspaces.

blocks.text: A **workspace** is the operational/collaboration environment where users actually work. Databricks describes it as the environment where workloads such as ingestion, interactive analysis, scheduled jobs and ML training run.
ACME might have one account with three workspaces: `analytics-prod`, `engineering-dev`, `research`.

blocks.title: Azure tenant mental model
blocks.text: **Azure tenant** ≈ organization-wide level; **Databricks account** ≈ organization-wide Databricks level; **workspace** ≈ a specific environment where teams and workloads operate. Not a perfect 1:1 mapping, but a useful mental model.

sections.title: Control Plane vs Compute Plane
sections.hook: Knowing which plane does what tells you where to look when something breaks.

blocks.text: Databricks architecture explicitly separates two planes: the **control plane** and the **compute plane**.

items.title: CONTROL PLANE — "manages and coordinates"
points: Web UI (the web app lives here)

blocks.title: Restaurant
blocks.text: The **control plane** is the front desk and manager: takes the order, schedules the kitchen, keeps the books. The **compute plane** is the kitchen where the food (your data) is actually cooked.
Follow one command. In a notebook you write:

blocks.code: df.groupBy("country").sum("amount").show()

blocks.text:
Browser
   │
   ▼
Databricks control services   (control plane)
   │  schedule / coordinate execution
   ▼
Compute plane
   ├── Driver / Spark session
   ├── Workers
   └── Photon / Spark execution
   │
   ▼
Data storage
blocks.caption: The path of one notebook command.

blocks.title: Who actually runs groupBy?
blocks.text: Your **browser does not** run the groupBy. The **control plane is not** where the Spark workload runs. The computation happens in the **compute plane**.

blocks.label: Think first: Browser → Databricks UI → Spark query → ADLS. Which two planes are involved?
blocks.text: The UI / platform coordination belongs to the **control plane**; the Spark computation happens in the **compute plane** (which then reads the data in ADLS storage).

sections.title: Classic vs Serverless Compute
sections.hook: Two compute planes, one fundamental trade-off: control vs convenience.

blocks.text: Today there are two main kinds of compute plane: the **classic compute plane** and the **serverless compute plane**. Databricks documentation separates them explicitly.
With **classic compute** you create and configure the resources yourself — a driver VM plus worker VMs — and choose many infrastructure characteristics.

Your cloud environment  (e.g. YOUR AWS account)
│
├── Driver VM
├── Worker VM
├── Worker VM
└── Worker VM
blocks.caption: Classic: resources live in the customer's cloud account (AWS; similar on Azure/GCP).

blocks.text: Classic = **more control**, but also **more operational responsibility**.
With **serverless** you say "I want compute to run this workload" — not "give me 1 driver with X RAM and 8 workers of this VM type". Databricks takes over most of the provisioning and scaling.

YOU: run notebook
        │
        ▼
Databricks
  ├── allocates compute
  ├── scales it
  ├── manages the runtime
  └── tears down / scales resources as appropriate

blocks.title: Current recommendation
blocks.text: Databricks today recommends **serverless compute for most interactive and automated workloads**, when it is available and supports your requirements.

blocks.title: Serverless ≠ "no servers"
blocks.text: Of course there are servers, CPUs and RAM. **Serverless** means *you* don't manage the underlying server infrastructure the same way — the **abstraction boundary moved**.

blocks.title: Not "serverless good, classic useless"
blocks.text: Some workloads **still need classic**. Serverless is a default recommendation, not a verdict that classic is obsolete.

blocks.title: Serverless limitations (current)
blocks.text: Serverless compute **does not support R**, **does not support Spark RDD APIs**, and is built on **Spark Connect** APIs. Old code like `spark.sparkContext.parallelize([1,2,3])` should not be assumed to work in a serverless notebook.

blocks.code: rdd = spark.sparkContext.parallelize([1, 2, 3])   # RDD API → needs classic compute
blocks.caption: Don't assume this runs on serverless.

blocks.text: **"Cluster" vs "compute"**: older tutorials say *cluster* everywhere; today's UI/docs prefer the broader word **compute**. Classic Spark compute still has the familiar shape:

DRIVER
              │
     ┌────────┼────────┐
     ▼        ▼        ▼
  worker   worker   worker

job → stage → task → partition
blocks.caption: Everything you know from Spark still applies on classic compute.

sections.title: Compute Types at a Glance: All-Purpose, Jobs, SQL Warehouse
sections.hook: There is no "the Databricks cluster" — there are compute types for different workload shapes.

blocks.text: **All-purpose compute** (classic) is used mostly for **interactive development**: several notebooks can attach to the same compute.

Notebook A ─┐
Notebook B ─┼──► All-purpose compute
Notebook C ─┘
blocks.caption: Good for development, interactive exploration, debugging.

blocks.title: All-purpose for automated jobs?
blocks.text: All-purpose compute is **not** Databricks' first recommendation for automated Jobs. For jobs it recommends **serverless** in most cases, or **classic jobs compute** when you need custom cluster characteristics.
**Jobs compute**: a pipeline runs at 02:00 (ingest → transform → aggregate). You don't need an interactive cluster open all day — compute exists for the job.

blocks.caption: Jobs compute lifecycle

blocks.text: Deeper later (Jobs chapters): serverless jobs, classic jobs compute, shared job compute, task-level compute.
A **SQL warehouse** is a compute resource **optimized for SQL analytics**, used by the SQL editor, dashboards, BI tools and other SQL workloads.

blocks.caption: A typical query a SQL warehouse executes.

blocks.text:
Power BI ─────┐
              │
SQL Editor ───┼──► SQL Warehouse ───► tables
              │
Dashboard ────┘

blocks.title: SQL warehouse ≠ database
blocks.text: Here **warehouse** means a **compute resource**, not the place where tables are stored. Tables keep their own data/storage layer; the warehouse only **executes queries**.

SQL warehouse types today: **Serverless**, **Pro**, **Classic**. There is also **Lakehouse Real-Time** (Beta) for specific low-latency/high-concurrency cases. For most SQL analytics, Databricks recommends a **serverless SQL warehouse** when available.

blocks.title: Why a SQL warehouse instead of general Spark compute?
blocks.text: *A SQL warehouse is purpose-built for SQL analytics and BI workloads and provides SQL-oriented performance, concurrency and scaling capabilities, whereas general notebook or classic compute is suited to broader Spark and programmatic workloads.*

sections.title: Databricks Runtime (DBR), LTS and Runtime ML
sections.hook: Hardware alone runs nothing: the Runtime is the software that makes compute behave a certain way.

blocks.text: You have a compute machine. Hardware alone is not enough — you need a **software environment**: Spark, Python, Scala, JVM, Delta libraries, Databricks integrations, optimized libraries, system dependencies.
Databricks packages a **tested software stack** called the **Databricks Runtime (DBR)**.

Compute VM            (hardware / infrastructure)
│
└── Databricks Runtime  (software)
      ├── Apache Spark
      ├── Delta support
      ├── Python environment
      ├── libraries
      ├── Databricks optimizations
      └── integrations

blocks.title: VM ≠ DBR
blocks.text: **VM / compute resources** = hardware/infrastructure abstraction. **DBR** = software runtime environment. Same VM type + different DBR can behave differently.

You will see versions like `17.3 LTS`, `18.x`, `19 Beta`. (In June 2026 the source reports DBR 19 Beta on Spark 4.2.0, with LTS lines like 17.3 and 16.4 still getting maintenance.) **Don't memorize numbers** — understand the consequence:

items.def: **Long-Term Support** runtime. Preferred in production when you want stability, predictable maintenance and less frequent migration instead of chasing every new release.

blocks.text: **Runtime debugging story**: DEV runs DBR 18.x, PROD runs DBR 17.3 LTS. `some_new_api(...)` works in dev but raises `AttributeError` in prod. Likely root cause: **runtime version mismatch**.

blocks.caption: Production debugging is never just "does the Python code have a bug?"

blocks.title: Ask yourself when code works in DEV but fails in PROD
questions: Which DBR version runs in DEV, and which in PROD?
Does the failing API/library exist in the older runtime?
Are the Python libraries/versions the same in both environments?
Is the configuration (compute, settings) the same?

blocks.text: **Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning (DBR ML)** adds prebuilt ML/DL infrastructure and common ML libraries so you don't build the whole environment yourself.

sections.title: Photon: The Vectorized Engine Under Your Code
sections.hook: Faster SQL/DataFrames without rewriting a single line.

blocks.text: **Spark** is an execution framework / engine ecosystem. **Photon** is the **Databricks-native vectorized query engine**, designed to accelerate SQL and DataFrame workloads.

blocks.title: What Photon is NOT
blocks.text: Photon is **not** another programming language, **not** a database and **not** a storage format.
The key point: you write the **same SQL/DataFrame code**. The optimization happens **beneath the API abstraction**.

blocks.code:
result = (
    spark.table("prod.sales.orders")
    .groupBy("country")
    .sum("amount")
)
# NOT: photon.groupBy(...)  ← no such API

blocks.label: Think first: why would processing a batch of values be faster than one row at a time?
blocks.text: Row-at-a-time pays per-row overhead (row 1 → process, row 2 → process…). **Vectorized** processing works on a batch `[v1 v2 v3 v4 …]` at once, exploiting CPU characteristics — less overhead, better CPU efficiency. (C++/SIMD internals come in the performance chapter.)

Row-at-a-time:   row1 → process
                 row2 → process
                 row3 → process

Vectorized:      [v1 v2 v3 v4 ...] → operate on the whole batch

blocks.title: Where Photon is on
blocks.text: Photon is **enabled on serverless compute and SQL warehouses**. On **classic** compute it is also available and usually enabled by default through the corresponding configuration.

blocks.title: What is Photon?
blocks.text: *Photon is Databricks' native vectorized execution engine that accelerates supported SQL and DataFrame operations underneath the existing APIs, so applications generally do not need a separate Photon-specific programming model.*

sections.title: Notebooks: Cells, Compute Attachment, display() vs show()
sections.hook: A notebook is a document — it does nothing until it is attached to compute.

blocks.text: A Databricks **notebook** is an interactive document made of **cells** — e.g. Cell 1 Python, Cell 2 SQL, Cell 3 Markdown, Cell 4 Python. Notebooks support **Python, SQL, Scala and R**, depending on the compute/runtime.

blocks.title: The notebook alone executes nothing
blocks.text: A notebook is a code/document **artifact**. Even `print("hello")` needs an **active execution session** on compute.

Notebook
   │  attach / connect
   ▼
Compute
   │
   ▼
execution
In **Unity Catalog-enabled workspaces**, Databricks can **auto-attach** a new notebook to **serverless compute** when you run a cell without having chosen other compute.
Your first real notebook cell:

blocks.code:
data = [
    (1, "Athens", 120.0),
    (2, "Volos", 80.0),
    (3, "Athens", 50.0),
    (4, "Patras", 200.0),
    (5, "Athens", 30.0),
]

df = spark.createDataFrame(
    data,
    ["order_id", "city", "amount"]
)

display(df)

blocks.text: You never created `spark` — in a Databricks notebook a ready-made **Spark session** exists on supported compute.

blocks.caption: Inferred schema: order_id: long · city: string · amount: double

items.title: display(df)
points: Not a core PySpark DataFrame method

blocks.title: Porting code out of Databricks
blocks.text: `display()` is a notebook convenience. If you move code outside Databricks (plain PySpark, a library, a test), `display` won't exist — use Spark APIs such as `df.show()`.

sections.title: Transformations, Physical Plans and Lazy Evaluation
sections.hook: Databricks doesn't hide your Spark knowledge — it leans on it.

blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

city_sales = (
    df
    .groupBy("city")
    .agg(
        F.sum("amount").alias("total_sales"),
        F.count("*").alias("orders")
    )
    .orderBy(F.desc("total_sales"))
)

display(city_sales)

head: city
total_sales
orders
blocks.caption: Athens = 120 + 50 + 30. (Athens and Patras tie at 200.0, so their relative order is not guaranteed.)

blocks.text: `groupBy("city")` most likely needs a **shuffle**, so that all rows with the same city key end up in the same downstream partition.

blocks.code:
city_sales.explain("formatted")
# or
city_sales.explain("extended")
blocks.caption: See the physical plan.

blocks.text:
HashAggregate   (final)
Exchange        ← redistribution / shuffle boundary
HashAggregate   (partial, per partition)
Sort
blocks.caption: Operators you will typically see for groupBy + orderBy.

blocks.title: Exchange = shuffle
blocks.text: In a physical plan, **Exchange** is usually where you see a redistribution/shuffle boundary.

blocks.label: Think first: why does `df.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)` usually need no shuffle, while `df.groupBy("city").sum("amount")` probably does?
blocks.text: A **filter** can be decided independently inside each existing partition (partition 1 → filter locally, partition 2 → filter locally…). For **groupBy("city")**, all rows with `city = Athens` must be combined logically even if they started in different partitions → **redistribution/shuffle**.
**What really happens when you press Run** (interview level):

items: Python runs in active compute session
Tasks process partitions (scan, filter, shuffle for groupBy)

blocks.text: **Lazy evaluation remains**: `orders = spark.table(...)`, `x = orders.filter(...)`, `y = x.groupBy(...).sum(...)` only **describe** computation.

blocks.code:
display(y)      # action
y.count()       # action
y.write...      # action
blocks.caption: These force evaluation. Databricks doesn't change this basic Spark logic.

blocks.title: filter() ≠ processed
blocks.text: After `df.filter(...)` no data has necessarily been processed yet: the transformation only extends the plan. Execution happens when an action/result is requested.

sections.title: Magic Commands, spark.table(), spark.sql() and _sqldf
sections.hook: One notebook, several languages — and they all meet at the same tables.

blocks.text: Say the notebook's **default language is Python**. A cell starting with **`%sql`** means: *interpret this cell as SQL*.

head: Magic
What the cell becomes
blocks.caption: Magic commands listed in the source.

blocks.code:
%python
x = 5
print(x * 2)

%sql
SELECT current_timestamp() AS now;

%md
# Sales Analysis
This is the daily sales notebook.
%pip install requests

blocks.title: %pip is notebook-scoped
blocks.text: `%pip` installs **notebook-scoped** Python libraries (scoped to the notebook/session context). Don't assume it is a permanent installation for the whole workspace.
**SQL and Python in the same flow**: both of these can point to the same logical table `main.sales.orders`.

blocks.caption: spark.table("catalog.schema.table")

blocks.code:
df = spark.sql("""
    SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM prod.silver.orders
    GROUP BY country
""")
display(df)
blocks.caption: spark.sql() returns a DataFrame: SQL statement → Spark SQL → DataFrame.

blocks.text: **`_sqldf`**: in supported notebook environments, the result of a `%sql` cell becomes available to **subsequent Python** code as `_sqldf`.

blocks.code:
%sql
SELECT * FROM prod.silver.orders WHERE amount > 100;
display(_sqldf)   # next Python cell: result of the SQL cell above

blocks.title: Interactive only
blocks.text: `_sqldf` is a handy interactive feature. **Don't build production architecture on it** — use `spark.sql()` / `spark.table()` and named DataFrames.

sections.title: Widgets and SQL Parameters (:param, IDENTIFIER)
sections.hook: Stop editing code to change a country — parameterize the notebook.

blocks.text: You want the notebook to run for different countries. **Bad**: `country = "GR"` and edit the code by hand each time.

blocks.code:
dbutils.widgets.dropdown(
    "country",          # name
    "GR",               # default value
    ["GR", "DE", "FR"], # choices
    "Country"           # label shown in the UI
)

country = dbutils.widgets.get("country")

filtered = (
    spark.table("prod.silver.orders")
    .filter(F.col("country") == country)
)
display(filtered)
blocks.caption: Create → read → use.

items.def: Notebook input controls for **parameterized notebooks/dashboards**. Types include **text**, **dropdown**, **combobox** (and others, e.g. multiselect).
Returns the widget's current value (as a string) to Python code.

blocks.text: **Modern SQL parameter markers** use **`:parameter`** — not the older **`${parameter}`**, which is **deprecated for DBR 15.2+**.

blocks.code: dbutils.widgets.text("country", "GR")
blocks.caption: Python cell

blocks.code:
%sql
SELECT *
FROM prod.silver.orders
WHERE country = :country;
blocks.caption: SQL cell — modern parameter marker

blocks.title: :country, not ${country}
blocks.text: Learn today's syntax, not old tutorials: `:country` is current; `${country}` is legacy/deprecated.

blocks.label: Think first: a widget holds `table = orders`. Why can't you just write `SELECT * FROM :table`?
blocks.text: A **parameter value** and a **SQL identifier** are different semantic categories. `WHERE country = :country` inserts a *value*; `FROM ...` needs an *identifier* (an object name). Use **`IDENTIFIER(:table_name)`** for parameterized object names.

blocks.code:
SELECT *
FROM IDENTIFIER(:table_name);

blocks.title: Value vs identifier
blocks.text: Parameter markers stand for **values**. For table/column/schema names use **`IDENTIFIER()`**. Literal vs identifier vs parameter vs expression is a frequent source of SQL bugs (covered in depth later).

sections.hook: Find data by clicking, confirm it by SQL — then create a real table.

catalog

prod

blocks.text: Catalog Explorer requires suitable privileges such as **BROWSE** and/or the corresponding **data access privileges** to see objects.

items.def: Shows the table's columns and data types.
Shows table-level details (format, location, size, number of files…).

blocks.code: CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dev_training.sales;

Unity Catalog

   ▼
dev_training.sales.orders

Delta

storage
blocks.caption: Connect the layers: UC names & governs, Delta formats, storage holds bytes.
A real table workflow — not a toy DataFrame living only in RAM.

blocks.code:
orders = spark.table("dev_training.sales.orders")

greek_orders = orders.filter(F.col("country") == "GR")
display(greek_orders)

(orders
  .groupBy("country")
  .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
  .display())          # if .display() isn't supported, use display(...)
blocks.caption: The same table from Python.

blocks.title: Compute lifetime ≠ data lifetime
blocks.text: If compute stops, your Delta table is **not** lost — it lives in persistent storage. Compute can come and go; data persists.
`prod.silver.orders` is a **Unity Catalog three-level namespace**: **catalog.schema.table**.
Good production habit: write **`catalog.schema.table`** instead of just `orders`.

blocks.label: Think first: your current context is `dev.sales` and you run `SELECT * FROM orders;`. What do you read?
blocks.text: You read **`dev.sales.orders`** — while you may have believed you were reading `prod.sales.orders`. No error, just the wrong data. Very dangerous.

blocks.code:
SELECT current_catalog();
SELECT current_schema();
blocks.caption: Check the current namespace.

blocks.title: Unqualified names resolve against the current context
blocks.text: A short name is resolved using the **current catalog and schema**. For production transformations prefer the fully qualified `prod.silver.orders`.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before running a query with a short table name
questions: What are current_catalog() and current_schema() right now?
Could the same table name exist in dev and prod?
Would a fully qualified name remove any doubt?

sections.hook: Find the failing layer first — don't jump to shuffles when the notebook isn't even attached.

blocks.text: A **notebook cell is stuck**. Don't start by inspecting Spark shuffle. First decide **which layer** the failure is in.

head: Case
Symptom
Layer
First move
rows: Which principal? USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA / SELECT?

blocks.caption: Case B: typo 'ordres' instead of 'orders' — or wrong catalog/schema.

blocks.title: Ask yourself on TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND
questions: Does SHOW TABLES IN <catalog>.<schema> list the table?
Did I spell the table name exactly (ordres vs orders)?

questions: Which principal am I (or is the job running as)?
Do I have USE CATALOG on the catalog?
Do I have USE SCHEMA on the schema?
Do I have SELECT on the table?

blocks.title: Wrong layer, wrong tool
blocks.text: A permission error is a **governance** problem — you don't look at Spark partitions. A `ModuleNotFoundError` is an **environment** problem — not a data problem.

blocks.code:
import some_library        # ModuleNotFoundError
%pip install some-library   # notebook fix
blocks.caption: Case D. In production, manage dependencies systematically, not with ad-hoc %pip.

blocks.title: Works when I run it, fails as a scheduled job
blocks.text: Notebook works for you, but the scheduled job gets `PERMISSION_DENIED`. First serious hypothesis: a **different execution identity/principal** runs the job.

blocks.title: Works in DEV, ModuleNotFoundError in PROD
blocks.text: Check early: (1) the **Databricks Runtime version**, (2) the **Python/library environment**.

sections.title: Slow Queries: Case E and the Debugging Tree
sections.hook: "It's slow, get a bigger cluster" is a guess, not a diagnosis.

blocks.text: **Case E — the query runs but is slow.** *Now* you start looking at Spark.

blocks.title: Slow ≠ small cluster
blocks.text: A slow query does **not** automatically mean the cluster is too small. That habit should disappear from day one.

result = (
    spark.table("prod.silver.orders")
    .join(spark.table("prod.silver.customers"), "customer_id")
    .groupBy("country")
    .agg(F.sum("amount"))
)
display(result)     # runs for 40 minutes

debug.title: Notebook cell stuck or won't run
debug.symptom: You press Run and the cell hangs, does nothing, or the notebook says it is not attached.
askYourself: Is the notebook attached to any compute at all?
Is that compute actually running?
Is the session healthy?
Did my code even parse?
Does the table I reference exist?
Do I have permission on it?
What does the query plan look like?
Is the problem in runtime execution itself?

steps.do: Check the compute selector at the top of the notebook; attach to serverless or start the compute.
steps.why: A notebook is only an artifact — without a session nothing executes (Case A).

steps.do: Re-run a trivial cell such as print("hello").
steps.why: Separates environment problems from code problems.

steps.do: Only if the environment is fine, check names (SHOW TABLES) and permissions.
steps.why: Next layers on the ladder: data/naming, then governance.

steps.do: Only then inspect the physical plan / Spark UI.
steps.why: Shuffle and skew analysis is the last layer, not the first.

rootCauses: Errors in later layers (names, permissions, plan)
debug.fix: Locate the failing layer top-down; for 'not attached' simply attach/start compute and re-run.
debug.mnemonic: Outside-in: Attach → Run → Session → Parse → Table → Permission → Plan → Execution

debug.title: TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND
debug.symptom: `spark.table("prod.silver.ordres")` or a SQL query fails with TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND.
askYourself: Does SHOW TABLES IN <catalog>.<schema> list this table?
Did I spell the name exactly right (ordres vs orders)?
Am I in the catalog/schema I think I am?
Did I use a fully qualified catalog.schema.table name?
Can I even see the catalog/schema (privileges)?

steps.do: List the tables in the schema.
steps.why: Confirms what actually exists.

steps.do: Compare the spelling character by character.
steps.why: Typos are the most common cause.

steps.do: Check the current namespace.
steps.why: Short names resolve against the current catalog/schema.

steps.do: Walk up: SHOW SCHEMAS IN prod; SHOW CATALOGS;
steps.why: The table may live in another schema/catalog.

steps.do: Rewrite with the fully qualified name and re-run.
steps.why: Removes namespace ambiguity.

rootCauses: Unqualified name resolved in the wrong context
debug.fix: Correct the name and use catalog.schema.table.

debug.title: INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES / PERMISSION_DENIED
debug.symptom: `SELECT * FROM prod.finance.transactions` fails with INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES — or a notebook that works for you fails as a scheduled job with PERMISSION_DENIED.
askYourself: Which principal am I — or which identity is the job running as?
Is the job running as a different identity than me?
Do I (does it) have USE CATALOG on the catalog?
Do I (does it) have USE SCHEMA on the schema?
Do I (does it) have SELECT on the table?

steps.do: Identify the executing principal (you vs the job's identity).
steps.why: Works-for-me / fails-as-job almost always means a different principal.

steps.do: Check USE CATALOG on the catalog.
steps.why: Outer privilege in the chain.

steps.do: Check USE SCHEMA on the schema.
steps.why: Middle privilege in the chain.

steps.do: Check SELECT on the table.
steps.why: The actual data access privilege.

debug.fix: Grant the missing privileges to the right principal (or run the job as an identity that has them). Do not look at Spark partitions — this is the governance layer.

debug.title: Works in DEV, fails in PROD (AttributeError / ModuleNotFoundError)
debug.symptom: Code runs on DEV (e.g. DBR 18.x) but PROD (e.g. DBR 17.3 LTS) raises AttributeError or ModuleNotFoundError.
askYourself: Which DBR version runs in DEV and which in PROD?
Does this API exist in the older runtime?
Are the Python libraries and their versions the same?
Was the library installed only notebook-scoped with %pip in DEV?
Is the compute configuration the same?

steps.do: Read the exact error and the failing call/import.
steps.why: AttributeError → API missing; ModuleNotFoundError → library missing.

steps.do: Compare the DBR versions of both environments.
steps.why: Different DBR = different Spark/Python/packages/capabilities.

steps.do: Compare installed libraries.
steps.why: `%pip` is notebook-scoped; PROD may not have the package.

steps.do: Compare configuration, then align runtime/dependencies.
steps.why: Production needs systematic dependency management, not ad-hoc installs.

debug.fix: Align DBR versions and manage dependencies systematically (or avoid APIs not present in the PROD runtime).

debug.title: Query runs but is slow
debug.symptom: A join + groupBy query (orders ⋈ customers → groupBy country) runs for 40 minutes.
askYourself: Is the compute actually healthy?
How much input data am I reading?
Which physical join did Spark choose — BHJ or SMJ?
Is there a huge shuffle (Exchange)?
Is the data skewed?
Are tasks spilling to disk?
Are there tiny files or a bad table layout?

steps.do: Rule out compute health problems.
steps.why: Environment first.

steps.do: Check input bytes and scans.
steps.why: Unnecessary scans are a common hidden cost.

steps.do: Read the physical plan for the join strategy.
steps.why: BHJ is usually reasonable; SMJ implies a shuffle.

steps.do: In the Spark UI look at shuffle size, task durations (skew) and spill.
steps.why: One very slow task = skew; spill = memory pressure.

steps.do: Check file sizes/layout.
steps.why: Tiny files or poor layout slow scans.

debug.fix: Fix the identified root cause; resize compute only if evidence shows a compute bottleneck.
debug.mnemonic: Slow ≠ small: Health → Input → Join → Shuffle → Skew → Spill → Files

debug.title: Query succeeds but returns the wrong data (wrong namespace)
debug.symptom: `SELECT * FROM orders` runs without error, but the numbers don't match production.
askYourself: What are current_catalog() and current_schema() right now?
Could a table with the same name exist in dev and prod?
Did I use a fully qualified name?
Did a previous USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA change my context?

steps.do: Check the current namespace.
steps.why: Short names resolve against it.

steps.do: Compare it with the intended environment.
steps.why: dev.sales.orders vs prod.sales.orders.

steps.do: Rewrite with catalog.schema.table.
steps.why: Eliminates ambiguity.

rootCauses: Unqualified name resolved in the wrong catalog/schema
debug.fix: Use fully qualified names in production transformations (or set USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA explicitly).

debug.title: Legacy RDD / R code fails on serverless
debug.symptom: `spark.sparkContext.parallelize([1,2,3])` (or R code) fails in a serverless notebook.
askYourself: Is this notebook running on serverless compute?
Does the failing line use RDD APIs / sparkContext or R?
Can I express it with the DataFrame API instead?
Do I truly need classic compute for this workload?

steps.do: Identify the failing construct.
steps.why: Serverless doesn't support RDD APIs or R; it's built on Spark Connect.

steps.do: Confirm the compute type.
steps.why: The same code may work on classic compute.

steps.do: Rewrite with DataFrames, or move the workload to classic compute.
steps.why: Both are valid; DataFrames keep you on the recommended path.

debug.fix: Modernize to DataFrame API or choose classic compute when RDD/R is required.

pitfalls.title: Databricks = managed Spark
pitfalls.text: Treating Databricks as just hosted Spark hides Delta, Unity Catalog, SQL warehouses, Lakeflow, Photon, serverless and more.
pitfalls.fix: Think platform (interfaces, compute, runtime, engine, governance) with Spark as the core engine.

pitfalls.title: Confusing account and workspace
pitfalls.text: The workspace is what you see daily, so people think it's the top level.
pitfalls.fix: Account = org level (identities, billing, policies, metastores, workspaces); workspace = collaboration environment.

pitfalls.title: Thinking the control plane runs your Spark job
pitfalls.text: The UI and coordination live in the control plane, but the browser/control plane don't do the groupBy.
pitfalls.fix: Data processing happens in the compute plane.

pitfalls.title: Serverless = no servers
pitfalls.text: There are still machines, CPUs and RAM.
pitfalls.fix: Serverless means Databricks manages provisioning and scaling — the abstraction boundary moved.

pitfalls.title: Serverless good, classic useless
pitfalls.text: Some workloads still need classic compute.
pitfalls.fix: Pick classic for R, RDD APIs or custom infra/network/runtime needs.

pitfalls.title: Assuming RDD code runs on serverless
pitfalls.text: `spark.sparkContext.parallelize` and R aren't supported on serverless (Spark Connect).
pitfalls.fix: Use the DataFrame API or classic compute.

pitfalls.title: Using all-purpose compute for automated jobs
pitfalls.text: All-purpose compute is meant for interactive development.
pitfalls.fix: Use serverless jobs (default) or classic jobs compute for custom needs.

pitfalls.title: SQL warehouse = database
pitfalls.text: A SQL warehouse doesn't store tables.
pitfalls.fix: It's SQL-optimized compute; tables live in storage.

pitfalls.title: "The Databricks cluster"
pitfalls.text: There isn't one cluster for everything.
pitfalls.fix: Choose compute by workload shape: notebook, SQL/BI, jobs, classic special cases.

pitfalls.title: DBR = VM
pitfalls.text: Mixing hardware and software layers.
pitfalls.fix: VM = infrastructure; DBR = software runtime stack.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring runtime mismatches
pitfalls.text: Code works in DEV (DBR 18.x) but fails in PROD (17.3 LTS) with AttributeError.
pitfalls.fix: Debug code + runtime + libraries + configuration together.

pitfalls.title: Photon misconceptions
pitfalls.text: Believing Photon is a language, database or storage format, or needs special code.
pitfalls.fix: Photon is a vectorized engine under the existing SQL/DataFrame APIs.

pitfalls.title: Notebook runs without compute
pitfalls.text: A notebook is just a document/artifact.
pitfalls.fix: Attach it to compute (UC workspaces can auto-attach serverless).

pitfalls.title: display() in portable code
pitfalls.text: `display()` is a Databricks notebook helper, not PySpark.
pitfalls.fix: Use `df.show()` or other Spark APIs in code that runs outside Databricks.

pitfalls.title: %pip is a permanent install
pitfalls.text: `%pip` installs notebook-scoped libraries only.
pitfalls.fix: Manage production dependencies systematically.

pitfalls.title: Building production on _sqldf
pitfalls.text: `_sqldf` is an interactive convenience.
pitfalls.fix: Use `spark.sql()`/named DataFrames in production code.

pitfalls.title: Using ${param}
pitfalls.text: Legacy parameter syntax, deprecated for DBR 15.2+.
pitfalls.fix: Use `:param` markers.

pitfalls.title: FROM :table
pitfalls.text: Parameter markers stand for values, not identifiers.
pitfalls.fix: Use `IDENTIFIER(:table_name)` for dynamic object names.

pitfalls.title: Unqualified table names
pitfalls.text: `orders` resolves against the current catalog/schema and can silently read dev.
pitfalls.fix: Use catalog.schema.table in production; check current_catalog()/current_schema().

pitfalls.title: Debugging the wrong layer
pitfalls.text: Jumping to shuffles when the notebook isn't attached, or to partitions on a permission error.
pitfalls.fix: Walk the layer ladder top-down.

pitfalls.title: Slow query → bigger cluster
pitfalls.text: Scaling without a root cause.
pitfalls.fix: Check plan, Spark UI, join strategy, shuffle, skew, spill, file layout first.

pitfalls.title: Compute stopped = data lost
pitfalls.text: Confusing compute lifetime with data lifetime.
pitfalls.fix: Delta tables live in persistent storage.

pitfalls.title: Transformation = processed
pitfalls.text: Lazy evaluation: `filter` only extends the plan.
pitfalls.fix: Execution happens on actions (display, count, write).

pitfalls.title: Works for me, fails as job
pitfalls.text: The job may run as a different principal.
pitfalls.fix: Check the job identity's USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA / SELECT.

exercises.q: Source Exercise 1 — which statement is correct?
options: Spark is one of the core execution technologies inside Databricks.
why: Databricks is a whole platform (UI, governance, SQL, orchestration…); Spark is one engine inside it.
Correct: Spark remains the central execution technology inside the platform.
Delta is the table format; Databricks is a platform.
AWS/Azure/GCP are cloud providers; Spark is an execution engine.
exercises.explain: Spark is an **execution engine**; Databricks is a **data/AI platform** that uses Spark (and Photon) to execute work. The tempting option A is the historical 'managed Spark' view, which is now an oversimplification.

exercises.q: "Databricks = managed Spark" is an accurate description of today's Databricks platform.
exercises.explain: Historically this was close; today it is the **most dangerous oversimplification**. Databricks also includes Delta Lake, Unity Catalog, SQL warehouses, Lakeflow, serverless compute, Photon, ML/AI services, orchestration and DevOps tooling — Spark is just the core execution technology.

exercises.q: Match each platform component to its role.
exercises.explain: These are the pieces that make Databricks a **platform** rather than 'just Spark'. Keeping each in its own bucket (format, governance, compute, engine, pipelines) is the whole point of this chapter.

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong?
exercises.explain: Spark and Photon are execution engines and a SQL warehouse is compute — all three **execute** work. **Unity Catalog** governs assets (names, metadata, permissions); it doesn't run queries.

exercises.q: In your own words: why is "Databricks is just managed Spark" an oversimplification, and what role does Spark still play?
exercises.model: Spark is still the central execution engine, but Databricks today is a unified data/AI platform: it adds Delta Lake (table format), Unity Catalog (governance), SQL warehouses (SQL compute), Lakeflow (pipelines), serverless compute, Photon (vectorized engine), ML/AI services, orchestration and DevOps tooling. So Spark is one technology inside the platform, not the platform itself.
rubric: Databricks = unified platform (engineering, analytics, AI, governance, deployment)
Names at least 3 non-Spark components (Delta, UC, SQL warehouses, Photon, Lakeflow, serverless…)
exercises.explain: A strong answer contrasts **engine** vs **platform** and lists concrete components beyond Spark.

exercises.q: Source Exercise 2 (extended) — where does each operation most likely happen?
exercises.explain: The **account** is the org-level boundary: identities, billing, policies, UC metastores, workspace creation. The **workspace** is where daily work happens: notebooks, jobs, queries, Catalog Explorer — and a Spark query is a workspace workload executed on compute.

exercises.q: Test Q1 — which is the higher organizational object?
why: A workspace lives inside an account.
Correct: one account can contain many workspaces.
A notebook lives inside a workspace.
Compute is execution infrastructure used from a workspace.
exercises.explain: The **account** sits at the top; it contains workspaces. The trap is thinking the workspace (what you see every day) is the top level.

exercises.q: A single Databricks account can contain multiple workspaces.
exercises.explain: Yes — e.g. ACME's one account can hold `analytics-prod`, `engineering-dev` and `research`. The reverse (one workspace containing accounts) is never true.

exercises.q: ACME's Databricks setup shows `analytics-prod`, `engineering-dev` and `research` under one account. What are they?
why: There is one account (the org boundary).
Correct: environments where teams and workloads operate.
Catalogs are data namespaces, not team environments.
Clusters are compute, not environments.
exercises.explain: Separate team/environment spaces like prod/dev/research are typically **workspaces** under a single **account**. Catalogs are data namespaces and clusters are compute — different layers.

exercises.q: Fill in the levels.
exercises.text: The [[account]] is the organization-level boundary where you manage identities, billing and workspaces. The [[workspace]] is the collaboration environment containing notebooks, jobs, dashboards and Catalog Explorer.
exercises.explain: Account = org-wide administration; workspace = where users work. Catalog, cluster and metastore belong to other layers (data namespace, compute, UC configuration).

exercises.q: The analogy "Azure tenant ≈ Databricks account, workspace ≈ a specific team environment" is an exact one-to-one mapping.
exercises.explain: The source explicitly says it is **not** an exact mapping — just a useful mental model for the org-wide vs environment-level distinction.

exercises.q: Sort each item into the plane it belongs to.
exercises.explain: The **control plane** 'manages and coordinates' (UI, APIs, metadata, configuration). The **compute plane** does the actual data processing (Spark, SQL, joins, ML).

exercises.q: Test Q2 — where does the real data processing happen?
why: The control plane coordinates; it doesn't run the Spark workload.
Correct.
The browser only shows the UI.
UC governs; it doesn't process data.
exercises.explain: Data processing (transformations, SQL, joins, aggregations, ML) runs on compute resources in the **compute plane**.

exercises.q: Test Q3 — the Databricks web UI conceptually belongs to…
exercises.explain: The web application lives in the **control plane**, together with APIs, metadata and orchestration. The compute plane is where data is processed.

exercises.q: When you run `df.groupBy("country").sum("amount").show()` in a notebook, your browser performs the aggregation.
exercises.explain: The browser only sends the command. The control plane coordinates, and the **compute plane** (driver + workers, Spark/Photon) executes the groupBy against storage.

exercises.q: Order the path of a notebook command from your keyboard to the data.
exercises.explain: Browser → control plane coordinates → compute plane executes (driver plans, workers run tasks) → data is read from/written to storage.

exercises.q: Test Q21 (hard) — `Browser → Databricks UI → Spark query → ADLS`. Which two planes take part, and how?
options: Control plane for UI/coordination; compute plane for the Spark computation
Compute plane for the UI; control plane for the Spark computation
Only the control plane — ADLS is part of it
Only the compute plane — the UI runs on the driver
why: Correct.
Exactly reversed.
ADLS is storage; the Spark computation still needs the compute plane.
The UI is a control-plane web app, not something running on the driver.
exercises.explain: UI and platform coordination = **control plane**; Spark computation = **compute plane**, which then reads data in ADLS storage.

exercises.q: Source Exercise 3 — interactive Python notebook with `spark.read.table(...)`, DataFrame transformations and SQL; no special infrastructure requirement. What does Databricks generally recommend today?
options: Serverless compute (if available and the workload is supported)
why: Fine but not the default recommendation without special needs.
Correct.
SQL warehouses serve SQL/BI, not Python notebooks.
Jobs compute is for automated jobs, not interactive work.
exercises.explain: Databricks recommends **serverless** for most interactive and automated workloads when available and supported. Classic is for special requirements (R, RDDs, custom config).

exercises.q: Test Q4 — "Serverless" means there are no servers involved.
exercises.explain: There are still CPUs, RAM and machines. Serverless means **Databricks manages** the provisioning/infrastructure for you — the abstraction boundary moved.

exercises.q: Test Q5 — valid reasons to choose classic instead of serverless (select all).
why: Correct: serverless doesn't support R today.
Correct: no RDD APIs on serverless (Spark Connect based).
Correct: classic gives custom configuration.
False: serverless runs SQL fine.
False: no such rule.
exercises.explain: Choose classic when you need capabilities/config serverless lacks: **R**, **RDD APIs**, or custom infra/network/runtime needs. 'Serverless = good, classic = useless' is wrong both ways.

exercises.q: This notebook runs on **serverless** compute. Which line should you not expect to work?
exercises.fix: Use the DataFrame API instead (e.g. `spark.createDataFrame([(1,),(2,),(3,)], ["n"])`) or run the notebook on classic compute if RDDs are truly required.
exercises.explain: Serverless is built on **Spark Connect** and does **not support RDD APIs** (`sparkContext`). DataFrame reads, filters and `display` are fine.

exercises.q: Serverless or classic? Sort each characteristic.
exercises.explain: The trade-off: serverless = less to manage, fast, auto-scaling; classic = more control and custom config, but more responsibility.

exercises.q: On AWS, classic compute resources (driver and worker VMs) live in the customer's AWS account.
exercises.explain: Yes — with classic compute the VMs run in **your** cloud environment (similar architectures exist on Azure and GCP). With serverless, Databricks manages the compute.

Confirm the notebook is running on serverless compute
Decide: rewrite with DataFrame API, or move to classic compute
exercises.explain: Locate the failing construct, confirm the compute type, then choose between modernizing the code and choosing classic compute.

exercises.q: Today's UI and docs mostly say "compute" where older tutorials said "cluster", but classic Spark compute still has a driver and workers.
exercises.explain: 'Compute' is the broader modern term. Classic compute still follows driver → workers, and job → stage → task → partition logic applies.

exercises.q: Compute-selection mental model — match the workload to the generally preferred compute.
exercises.explain: This is the current Databricks recommendation pattern: serverless where possible, the SQL warehouse for SQL/BI, and classic when you need unsupported features or custom config.

exercises.q: A SQL warehouse is where your tables' data is physically stored.
exercises.explain: Classic exam/interview trap. A SQL warehouse is **compute** that executes queries; tables keep their own storage layer (Delta files in cloud storage).

exercises.q: Test Q7 — which compute would you typically use for Power BI SQL queries?
exercises.explain: BI tools send SQL to a **SQL warehouse** — usually **serverless** when available. Notebook/all-purpose compute is for programmatic work.

exercises.q: Test Q8 — what is a SQL warehouse?
why: Correct.
Storage is a separate layer.
That's a schema (namespace).
Dashboards *use* a warehouse.
exercises.explain: A SQL warehouse is **SQL-optimized compute** used by the SQL editor, dashboards and BI tools — not storage.

exercises.q: Which is NOT a SQL warehouse type?
exercises.explain: Warehouse types are **Serverless, Pro, Classic** (plus Lakehouse Real-Time in Beta for low-latency/high-concurrency). **Photon** is an execution engine that runs inside warehouses.

exercises.q: Databricks' first recommendation for automated jobs is classic all-purpose compute.
exercises.explain: All-purpose compute is for interactive development. For jobs Databricks recommends **serverless** in most cases, or **classic jobs compute** when you need custom cluster characteristics.

exercises.q: A nightly 02:00 pipeline runs on jobs compute. Order its lifecycle.
exercises.explain: Jobs compute exists for the job — no interactive cluster sitting open all day.

exercises.q: Test Q6 — default recommendation for an interactive Python/DataFrame notebook?
exercises.explain: Interactive Python/DataFrames → **serverless notebook compute** generally preferred. SQL warehouses serve SQL/BI; jobs compute serves automation.

exercises.q: Interview Q28: "Why would you choose a SQL warehouse instead of general-purpose Spark compute?"
exercises.model: A SQL warehouse is purpose-built for SQL analytics and BI workloads and provides SQL-oriented performance, concurrency and scaling capabilities, whereas general notebook or classic compute is suited to broader Spark and programmatic workloads.
rubric: General compute suits broader Spark/programmatic workloads
exercises.explain: Hit the three axes: purpose (SQL/BI), properties (performance, concurrency, scaling) and contrast (programmatic Spark work).

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong with the others?
exercises.explain: The first three are **compute** types. **DBR 17.3 LTS** is the software/runtime environment that runs *on* compute.

exercises.q: Test Q9 — what is the Databricks Runtime?
options: The software/runtime stack (Spark + Databricks-integrated libraries and dependencies) the workload runs on
The VM type of the driver
exercises.explain: DBR is a **tested software stack**: Spark, Python, JVM, Delta support, libraries, optimizations, integrations. The VM is hardware; DBR is software.

exercises.q: Test Q10 — DBR and the VM are the same thing.
exercises.explain: **VM/compute resources** = hardware/infrastructure abstraction; **DBR** = software runtime environment installed on it.

exercises.q: DEV compute runs DBR 18.x, PROD runs DBR 17.3 LTS. `some_new_api(...)` works in DEV but PROD raises `AttributeError`.

options.text: Runtime version mismatch: the API doesn't exist in 17.3
options.fb: Different DBR = different Spark/Python/packages = different capabilities.

options.text: The PROD cluster is too small
options.fb: Size doesn't remove attributes from an API.

options.text: A typo in the table name
options.fb: That would be TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND, not AttributeError.
Permissions give INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES, not AttributeError.

options.text: Compare DBR versions, libraries and configuration across DEV and PROD
options.fb: Production debugging = code + runtime + libraries + configuration.

options.text: Compare row counts of the tables
options.fb: This is an environment failure, not a data issue.
Photon doesn't add or remove Python attributes.

exercises.explain: When code behaves differently across environments, align the **runtime, libraries and configuration** before suspecting the code.

exercises.q: Order the investigation of "works in DEV, AttributeError in PROD".
items: Read the exact error and the failing call
Compare DBR versions in DEV vs PROD
Align the runtime (or avoid the newer API) and re-test
exercises.explain: Start from the error, then walk the environment layers: runtime → libraries → configuration, and fix by aligning environments.

exercises.q: Fill in the runtime terms.
exercises.text: LTS stands for [[Long-Term Support]]. For production, LTS is often preferred for stability, predictable maintenance and less frequent [[migration|migrations]]. DBR ML = standard DBR + [[ML libraries|machine learning libraries]] + ML/DL infrastructure.
exercises.explain: LTS runtimes trade newest features for stability; DBR ML saves you from building an ML environment yourself.

exercises.q: What can change when you switch DBR version? (select all)
options: The data stored in your Delta tables
exercises.explain: Different DBR → different Spark, packages, capabilities, bug fixes and behavior. Your **stored data** doesn't change just because the runtime changed.

exercises.q: Match the term to what it is.
exercises.explain: Keep hardware (VM) separate from software (DBR), and know the two DBR flavors that matter now: LTS for stability, ML for prebuilt ML tooling.

exercises.q: Why is production debugging "code + runtime + libraries + configuration" and not just "does the Python code have a bug?"
exercises.model: The same code can behave differently depending on the Databricks Runtime (Spark/Python versions, available APIs), the installed libraries and the configuration. A failure in PROD may come from a runtime mismatch (e.g. DBR 18.x in dev vs 17.3 LTS in prod) or a missing library, even if the code is correct.
rubric: Same code, different environment → different behavior
Example such as AttributeError from version mismatch
exercises.explain: The point is to widen your search space from 'my code' to the whole execution environment.

exercises.q: Source Exercise 4 — to use Photon you must rewrite `df.groupBy("customer_id").sum("amount")` with a Photon-specific API.
exercises.explain: No. The same DataFrame/SQL abstraction can execute through Photon for supported operations — optimization happens **beneath** the API.

exercises.q: Photon IS one of these — which one?
exercises.explain: Photon is a **Databricks-native vectorized query engine**. It is not a language, not a database and not a storage format — the three classic misconceptions.

exercises.q: Where is Photon available?
options: Enabled on serverless compute and SQL warehouses; also available (usually on by default) on classic compute
Only on classic compute with a special Photon library
Only when you import the photon module
exercises.explain: Photon is **enabled on serverless and SQL warehouses**, and on classic compute it's available and usually enabled by default via configuration. There is no module to import.

exercises.q: Someone tried to 'turn on Photon' in code. Which line is wrong?
lines: from pyspark.sql import functions as F
exercises.explain: There is no `photon.groupBy` API. You write normal DataFrame/SQL code and Photon accelerates supported operations underneath.

exercises.q: Interview Q29: "What is Photon?"
exercises.model: Photon is Databricks' native vectorized execution engine that accelerates supported SQL and DataFrame operations underneath the existing APIs, so applications generally do not need a separate Photon-specific programming model.
rubric: Works under existing APIs — no special code
exercises.explain: Nail the three points: what (vectorized native engine), for what (SQL/DataFrames), how you use it (you don't change code).

exercises.q: Why can vectorized processing be faster than row-at-a-time?
options: It processes batches of values at once, reducing per-row overhead and using CPU characteristics better
It skips rows that don't match
It stores data in a different file format
exercises.explain: Vectorized execution operates on **batches** (`[v1 v2 v3 …]`) instead of one row at a time, cutting overhead and improving CPU efficiency. It is not a storage format and doesn't change cluster size.

exercises.q: Complete the definition.
exercises.text: Photon is a Databricks-native [[vectorized]] query engine that accelerates [[SQL]] and [[DataFrame]] workloads, while Spark is the broader execution framework.
exercises.explain: Vectorized + SQL/DataFrame is the core of the definition. RDD workloads are not what Photon targets.

exercises.q: Test Q19 — a notebook that exists but is not attached to any compute can still execute a Spark workload.
exercises.explain: A notebook is an artifact/interface. It needs an **execution compute/session** — even `print("hello")` needs one.

exercises.q: Spark API or Databricks notebook/platform helper?
exercises.explain: Spark APIs work anywhere Spark runs. `display`, `dbutils` and `_sqldf` are **notebook/platform conveniences** — they break if you port code outside Databricks.

exercises.q: `spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Athens", 120.0), …], ["order_id", "city", "amount"])` — which schema is inferred?
options: order_id: long, city: string, amount: double
order_id: int, city: string, amount: float
order_id: string, city: string, amount: string
order_id: long, city: string, amount: decimal(10,2)
exercises.explain: Python ints become **long** and Python floats become **double**. DECIMAL only appears when you declare it (as in a SQL table definition).

exercises.q: Create a Spark DataFrame `df` from the list `data` with columns `order_id`, `city`, `amount`, and render it with the Databricks notebook helper.
exercises.explain: In a Databricks notebook `spark` already exists. `display(df)` gives rich rendering; `df.show()` would be the portable Spark alternative.

exercises.q: This script will run as a **plain PySpark job outside Databricks**. Which line will fail?
exercises.explain: `display()` is a **Databricks notebook helper**, not a PySpark method. Outside Databricks use `df.show()`. (Outside Databricks you *do* need to build the SparkSession, as lines 0–1 do.)

exercises.q: In a Unity Catalog-enabled workspace you open a brand-new notebook and run a cell without choosing compute. What can happen?
options: Databricks can automatically attach it to serverless compute
The cell runs in your browser
The cell silently does nothing forever
A SQL warehouse is created for it
exercises.explain: Current Databricks can **auto-attach** new notebooks to **serverless compute** in UC-enabled workspaces. Code never runs in the browser.

exercises.q: In a Databricks notebook you must create `spark` yourself with `SparkSession.builder` before using it.
exercises.explain: A ready-made Spark session (`spark`) is provided on supported compute. You only build it yourself outside Databricks.

exercises.q: Orders: (1, Athens, 120.0), (2, Volos, 80.0), (3, Athens, 50.0), (4, Patras, 200.0), (5, Athens, 30.0). What is `total_sales` for Athens?
exercises.explain: 120 + 50 + 30 = **200.0**, from 3 orders. Note Patras also has 200.0, so in `orderBy(desc("total_sales"))` Athens and Patras tie and their order isn't guaranteed.

exercises.q: Source Exercise 5 — why does `df.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)` usually need no shuffle, while `df.groupBy("city").sum("amount")` probably does?
options: Filter is decided independently within each partition; groupBy must bring all rows of the same city together across partitions
Filter runs on the driver; groupBy runs on workers
groupBy writes to disk; filter doesn't
exercises.explain: Each partition can filter **locally**. But rows with `city = Athens` may sit in several partitions and must be combined logically → **redistribution/shuffle**.

exercises.q: What happens when you press Run on a cell with transformations + `display(result)`? Put the steps in order.
items: Python code executes in the active compute session
Spark/Photon execution: tasks process partitions (scan, filter, shuffle)
exercises.explain: Not just 'Python runs': code builds a lazy plan, an action triggers Catalyst optimization, a physical plan is chosen, and Spark/Photon tasks process partitions.

exercises.q: Which of these trigger actual evaluation? (select all)
exercises.explain: `display`, `count` and `write` are **actions** needing a result. `filter` and `groupBy().sum()` are **transformations** that only describe computation (lazy evaluation).

exercises.q: Complete the code to print the physical plan in the readable format, and name the shuffle operator.
exercises.text:
city_sales.[[explain]]("[[formatted|extended]]")
# shuffle boundary operator in the plan: [[Exchange]]
exercises.explain: `explain("formatted")` (or `"extended"`) shows the plan. **Exchange** marks redistribution/shuffle; you'll also see HashAggregate and Sort.

exercises.q: Test Q26 — `spark.table("orders").groupBy("customer_id").sum("amount")` shows **Exchange** in the plan. What does that most likely mean?
options: Data redistribution/shuffle is required for the aggregation
Data is being exchanged with the control plane
The table is being copied to a new location
exercises.explain: Exchange = **shuffle**: rows with the same `customer_id` must meet in the same partition. This is your Spark knowledge applied directly in Databricks.

exercises.q: Test Q20 — once `df.filter(...)` has run in a cell, the data has already been filtered.
exercises.explain: Because of **lazy evaluation**, the filter only adds to the computation plan. Execution happens when an action/result is requested (display, count, write).

exercises.q: How many rows will `city_sales` (groupBy city over the 5 orders in Athens/Volos/Patras) contain?
exercises.explain: One row per distinct city: Athens, Patras, Volos → **3** rows. groupBy collapses the 5 orders into 3 groups.

exercises.q: Write `city_sales`: group `df` by `city`, compute `total_sales` (sum of amount) and `orders` (count of rows), sorted by `total_sales` descending.
exercises.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

city_sales = (
    df
    .groupBy("city")
    .agg(
        F.sum("amount").alias("total_sales"),
        F.count("*").alias("orders")
    )
    .orderBy(F.desc("total_sales"))
)
exercises.explain: `agg` with aliased `F.sum`/`F.count`, then `orderBy(F.desc(...))`. Expect HashAggregate + Exchange in the plan.

exercises.q: Interview: explain what really happens between pressing Run and seeing a table from `display(result)`.
exercises.model: The cell's Python runs in the active compute session. The DataFrame calls build a lazy logical plan; nothing is processed yet. display() is an action, so Spark runs Catalyst analysis/optimization, picks a physical plan, and Spark/Photon executes it as tasks over partitions — scanning, filtering, and shuffling for the groupBy — and returns the result to the notebook.
rubric: Runs in compute session, not browser
Physical plan executed by Spark/Photon tasks over partitions
exercises.explain: The interview-level answer connects notebook → lazy plan → action → Catalyst → physical plan → distributed tasks.

exercises.q: Test Q15/Q16 (extended) — match each magic command to what it does.
exercises.explain: Magic commands switch how **one cell** is interpreted (`%python`, `%sql`, `%scala`, `%r`, `%md`) or manage notebook-scoped libraries (`%pip`).

exercises.q: `%pip install requests` permanently installs `requests` for every notebook in the workspace.
exercises.explain: `%pip` installs **notebook-scoped** libraries tied to the notebook/session context — not a permanent workspace-wide installation.

exercises.q: A cell in a Python-default notebook should run this query as SQL, but it fails with a Python SyntaxError. Which line is wrong?
exercises.fix:
%sql
SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM prod.silver.orders
GROUP BY city;
exercises.explain: The magic `%python` tells the notebook to parse SQL text as Python. Start the cell with **`%sql`** so it's interpreted as SQL.

exercises.q: Test Q13 — what does `spark.table("prod.silver.orders")` do?
options: Creates a Spark DataFrame that refers to that table object
Copies the whole table into driver memory
Opens the table in Catalog Explorer
exercises.explain: It resolves the UC name's metadata and returns a **DataFrame** pointing at the table. Thanks to lazy evaluation, nothing is read until an action runs.

exercises.q: What does `spark.sql("SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM prod.silver.orders GROUP BY country")` return?
options: Nothing — it only runs the query
exercises.explain: SQL statement → Spark SQL → **DataFrame**. You can keep transforming it or `display()` it.

exercises.q: From Python, run SQL that computes revenue per country from `prod.silver.orders` into DataFrame `df`, then display it.
exercises.solution:
df = spark.sql("""
    SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM prod.silver.orders
    GROUP BY country
""")
display(df)
exercises.explain: `spark.sql` lets you write SQL while staying in Python and getting a DataFrame back.

exercises.q: What is `_sqldf`, and how should you use it?
options: The result of the previous SQL cell exposed to subsequent Python; a handy interactive feature, not a basis for production design
A built-in table listing all SQL queries; ideal for production auditing
A function that converts a DataFrame to SQL
exercises.explain: In supported notebook environments, a `%sql` cell's result becomes `_sqldf` for later Python cells. Great for exploration — but use `spark.sql()`/named DataFrames in production.

exercises.q: Complete the two cells so a SQL result is reused in Python.
exercises.text:
%[[sql]]
SELECT * FROM prod.silver.orders WHERE amount > 100;

# next cell (Python)
display([[_sqldf]])
exercises.explain: `%sql` makes the cell SQL; its result is exposed to later Python as `_sqldf` in supported environments.

exercises.q: `spark.table("main.sales.orders")` in Python and `%sql SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders` can lead to the same logical table.
exercises.explain: Both resolve the same Unity Catalog name. Python and SQL are just two front doors to the same table.

exercises.q: Complete the dropdown widget and read its value.
exercises.explain: `dropdown(name, default, choices, label)` creates the control; `dbutils.widgets.get(name)` returns its current value.

exercises.q: Test Q17 — which is today's SQL parameter marker syntax for a widget named `country`?
why: Correct: modern parameter marker.
Legacy; deprecated for DBR 15.2+.
Not Databricks parameter syntax here.
Not this syntax.
exercises.explain: Use **`:country`**. `${country}` is the older syntax, deprecated for DBR 15.2+ — learn today's syntax, not old tutorials.

exercises.q: Which line uses deprecated syntax?
exercises.explain: `${country}` is legacy/deprecated (DBR 15.2+). The modern parameter marker is `:country`.

exercises.q: A widget holds a table name. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: A parameter marker stands for a **value**; after `FROM` SQL needs an **identifier**. Wrap it: `IDENTIFIER(:table_name)`.

exercises.q: Test Q18 — why isn't `FROM :table` treated like `WHERE country = :country`?
options: `FROM` needs a SQL identifier (object name), while `WHERE country = :country` takes a parameter value
Parameters only work in Python cells
`:table` is reserved syntax for temporary views
exercises.explain: Identifier vs value are different semantic categories. For dynamic object names use `IDENTIFIER()`.

exercises.q: Create a text widget `country` with default `GR` (Python), then write the SQL cell that filters `prod.silver.orders` with the modern parameter marker.
exercises.solution:
dbutils.widgets.text("country", "GR")

%sql
SELECT *
FROM prod.silver.orders
WHERE country = :country;
exercises.explain: Create the widget once, then reference it in SQL with `:country` (not `${country}`).

exercises.q: Order the parameterized-notebook pattern.
items: Use the value in a filter
exercises.explain: Create → get → use → display. Users then change the widget instead of editing code.

exercises.q: Can a plain parameter marker (`:p`) go there, or do you need `IDENTIFIER(:p)`?

items.text: Catalog/schema name in a qualified name

exercises.explain: Values (strings, numbers, dates) use plain markers. Anything that is an **object name** (table, column, schema) is an identifier → `IDENTIFIER()`.

exercises.q: The `${param}` syntax is deprecated for DBR 15.2 and above.
exercises.explain: Correct. Modern SQL uses parameter markers like `:param`.

exercises.q: Why are widgets better than writing `country = "GR"` at the top of the notebook?
exercises.model: Hardcoding means editing code every time you need another country, which is error-prone and not reusable. Widgets turn the notebook into a parameterized notebook/dashboard: the value is chosen in the UI (or passed in), read with dbutils.widgets.get, and the code stays unchanged.
rubric: Avoids editing code for each run
exercises.explain: Widgets separate **inputs** from **logic** — the first step toward reusable, schedulable notebooks.

exercises.q: Order the SQL drill-down from the top of the namespace to one table's details.
exercises.explain: Catalog → schema → table → columns → table-level details. This drill-down is your basic debugging toolkit.

exercises.q: Complete the exploration commands.
exercises.explain: SHOW CATALOGS / SCHEMAS IN catalog / TABLES IN catalog.schema, and DESCRIBE DETAIL for table-level info (format, location, size).

exercises.q: Create the schema `dev_training.sales` only if missing, then a Delta table `orders` with order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2), country STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP.
keywords: create schema if not exists dev_training.sales
exercises.explain: Schema first (catalog.schema), then the table with a fully qualified name and `USING DELTA`.

exercises.q: The table has 5 columns (order_id, customer_id, amount, country, order_ts). Which line breaks the INSERT?
exercises.explain: Row 2 has only 4 values — the `country` value is missing. Every VALUES row must match the table's column count and order.

exercises.q: Test Q22 — the compute stopped, so your Delta table is gone.
exercises.explain: **Compute lifetime ≠ data lifetime.** The Delta table lives in persistent storage; compute can stop and start without affecting it.

exercises.q: A colleague can't see the `prod` catalog in Catalog Explorer, but you can. Most likely reason?
options: They lack privileges such as BROWSE or the corresponding data access privileges
Catalog Explorer only shows the creator's objects
exercises.explain: Catalog Explorer discovery is **governed**: you need privileges like **BROWSE** and/or data access privileges. Compute size and Photon are irrelevant to visibility.

exercises.q: Match each layer to its job for `dev_training.sales.orders`.
exercises.explain: UC names and governs, Delta formats, storage persists, compute executes — four separate layers.

exercises.q: You want table-level information such as format, location and number of files. Which command?
exercises.explain: `DESCRIBE DETAIL` gives table-level details; `DESCRIBE TABLE` gives columns and types; SHOW commands list objects.

exercises.q: Test Q14 — what is each part of `prod.silver.orders`?
exercises.explain: Unity Catalog's three-level namespace: **catalog.schema.table**.

exercises.q: Current context is `dev.sales`. You run `SELECT * FROM orders;` believing you read production. What do you actually read?
options: An error: the name is ambiguous
exercises.explain: Short names resolve against the **current catalog and schema** → `dev.sales.orders`. No error — just silently wrong data. Use fully qualified names.

exercises.q: Your notebook's revenue numbers are far lower than finance's report. The query is `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders;` and it runs without errors.

options.fb: The unqualified name may be resolving to a different catalog/schema.
Wrong numbers aren't a performance problem.
Photon changes speed, not results.
No dependency error here.

options.text: Rewrite with the fully qualified name prod.sales.orders (or USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA explicitly)
options.fb: Fully qualified names remove the ambiguity.
Destructive and doesn't fix the habit.
Same context → same wrong table.

exercises.explain: Silent wrong-namespace reads are dangerous because nothing errors. Check the current namespace and fully qualify production queries.

exercises.q: Order the steps when you suspect a short table name hit the wrong environment.
items: Notice results look wrong (no error raised)
exercises.explain: Confirm the current namespace, compare with intent, and fix by fully qualifying.

exercises.q: Check and set the namespace.
exercises.explain: `current_catalog()`/`current_schema()` reveal the context; `USE CATALOG`/`USE SCHEMA` set it.

exercises.q: An unqualified table name like `orders` is always resolved in the `prod` catalog.
exercises.explain: It's resolved against the **current** catalog and schema, whatever they are. That's why production code should use `catalog.schema.table`.

exercises.q: Set the context to catalog `prod` and schema `silver`, then select all rows from `orders` using the short name.
exercises.explain: After `USE CATALOG`/`USE SCHEMA`, `orders` resolves to `prod.silver.orders`. For production transformations, the fully qualified name is still safer.

exercises.q: `spark.table("prod.silver.ordres")` fails with `TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND`.

options.fb: List what actually exists in that schema.

options.text: Open the Spark UI and inspect shuffles
options.fb: Wrong layer — the plan never ran; the name didn't resolve.
Compute size can't create a missing name.
Tables aren't packages.
Fix the name and re-run.
Permission errors look like INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES.
Runtime issues show up as AttributeError/ModuleNotFoundError.

steps.prompt: If `orders` had NOT been listed there, what would you check next?

options.text: Whether I'm in the wrong catalog/schema (current_catalog(), current_schema(), SHOW SCHEMAS)
options.fb: The table may live elsewhere.
Doesn't change where tables live.
Irrelevant to name resolution.

exercises.explain: TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND is a **naming/namespace** problem: typo or wrong catalog/schema. Use SHOW TABLES/SCHEMAS before touching Spark internals.

exercises.q: A notebook cell is stuck/failing. Order the layer ladder (top to bottom).
exercises.explain: Find the failing **layer** first: environment → code → data/naming → governance → plan → execution. Don't jump to shuffle analysis when the notebook isn't even attached.

exercises.q: Which layer does each symptom point to?

items.text: AttributeError only on the older DBR

exercises.explain: Classify before you fix: Case A environment, Case B naming, Case C governance, Case D runtime/dependency.

exercises.q: Test Q25 — the notebook works when **you** run it, but the scheduled job fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED`.

options.text: The job runs as a different execution identity/principal
options.fb: Same code, different principal → different privileges.

options.text: The job's cluster is too small
options.fb: Size doesn't cause permission errors.
Then you'd see TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND, and it works for you.

options.text: Photon is off on job compute
options.fb: Photon doesn't affect authorization.

steps.prompt: What do you verify for that principal?

options.text: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the objects
options.fb: The full privilege chain must exist for the job's principal.
Wrong layer — this is governance.
Runtime doesn't grant permissions.

exercises.explain: When it works for you but not for the job, compare **who** runs it. Then check the privilege chain for that principal.

exercises.q: Case C — order the questions for `INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES` on `SELECT * FROM prod.finance.transactions`.
items: Which principal am I (or is the job running as)?
Do I have USE CATALOG on prod?
Do I have USE SCHEMA on prod.finance?
Do I have SELECT on the table?
exercises.explain: Identity first, then the chain from outer to inner: catalog → schema → table. This is the governance layer — not Spark partitions.

exercises.q: Test Q24 — notebook works in DEV but PROD shows `ModuleNotFoundError`. Which two categories do you check early? (select all that apply)
exercises.explain: ModuleNotFoundError is a **runtime/environment/dependency** issue: compare DBR versions and the installed Python libraries. Grants and shuffles belong to other layers.

exercises.q: This cell raises `TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND`. Which line?

exercises.q: Task A — SQL: revenue per city from `dev_training.sales.orders`, highest first.
exercises.solution:
SELECT
  city,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM dev_training.sales.orders
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
exercises.explain: Aggregate with SUM, group by city, sort descending by the alias.

exercises.q: Task B — PySpark: the same result as Task A in a DataFrame `city_revenue`, displayed.
exercises.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders = spark.table("dev_training.sales.orders")
city_revenue = (
    orders
    .groupBy("city")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
    .orderBy(F.desc("revenue"))
)
display(city_revenue)
exercises.explain: Same logic, DataFrame API: `spark.table` → `groupBy` → `agg(F.sum().alias())` → `orderBy(F.desc())`.

exercises.q: Interview Q27: "What is the difference between a Databricks workspace and compute?"
exercises.model: A workspace is the collaborative and operational environment that contains development, orchestration, governance and analytics interfaces, whereas compute is the execution infrastructure used to actually process workloads submitted from those interfaces.
rubric: Workloads are submitted from the workspace and processed on compute
exercises.explain: Interfaces vs execution: the workspace is where you work; compute is what does the work.
